summary: Specifies a new type, the Key ID Information Type, for the General Extension Payload of the Multimedia Internet KEYing protocol. It is used, for example, in the 3GPP Multimedia Broadcast/Multicast Service. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: When many people share secret keys, each key needs a name tag. This adds a new kind of name tag to a key-sharing message so the receiver knows which key to use.

subtitle: A new MIKEY extension that labels which kind of key, and which specific key, a message is carrying.

tldr.problem: The 3GPP multicast and broadcast service updates its keys frequently and needs a way to say which type of key, and which key, a MIKEY message carries.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds Type 3, the Key ID Information type, to the MIKEY General Extension Payload. It holds one or more sub-payloads, each giving a key ID type, a length and the key ID. It also registers an empty map type for security policy sent outside MIKEY.
tldr.outcome: The RFC warns that the MTK delivery it supports is protected by a group MAC, not source authenticated, so group members could spoof updates. It has since been updated by RFC 6309.

today: RFC 4563 is a Proposed Standard that has been updated by RFC 6309. Read the update alongside it for the current state of this extension.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Third Generation Partnership Project (3GPP) was developing a multicast and broadcast service, the Multimedia Broadcast/Multicast Service (MBMS). It uses the Multimedia Internet KEYing protocol (MIKEY, RFC 3830) to carry the keys and related security parameters for protecting multicast or broadcast media.

MBMS requires frequent key updates. The reasoning is that it should cost more to redistribute decryption keys to non-subscribers over the unicast channel than it costs to purchase the keys. To do this, MBMS uses three-level key management, so it can re-key by pushing down a new group key.

MBMS therefore needs to identify which types of keys are in a MIKEY message and what their identities are. This memo defines a new type for the MIKEY General Extension Payload to do that.
sections.plainLanguage: A TV service changes its secret keys often so that people who stop paying cannot keep watching. Each key needs a label, and this RFC defines the label format.

sections.title: The Three-Level Key Scheme
sections.content:
MBMS uses three kinds of key. The MBMS User Key (MUK) is a point-to-point key between the multicast server and each client. The MBMS Service Key (MSK) is a group key shared by the server and all clients. The MBMS Traffic Key (MTK) is the group traffic key, and it is the one that is regularly updated.

The MUK is a pre-shared key. It is used to run MIKEY with the pre-shared key method and to deliver the MSK point to point. The same MSK is pushed to all clients as a second-level group key. The MSK is then used to push an MTK to all clients. The MTK protects the media traffic, and could be, for example, the master key for SRTP in the streaming case.

A Key Domain identifier says where group keys are valid, for example a specific service provider.
sections.plainLanguage: There is a private key for each person, a club key for the whole group, and a daily key for the show. The private key delivers the club key, and the club key delivers the daily key.

sections.title: How This Fits MIKEY and GKMARCH
sections.content:
According to RFC 3830, MIKEY is a registration protocol that supports re-keying for unicast in the terms of the MSEC Group Key Management Architecture (RFC 4046). MBMS uses MIKEY both as a registration protocol and as a re-key protocol.

The extension in this RFC supplies the additions to RFC 3830 that let MIKEY work as both a unicast and a multicast re-key protocol in the MBMS setting.
sections.plainLanguage: MIKEY already knew how to hand a key to one person. This add-on lets it also announce new keys to a whole crowd.

sections.title: The Key ID Information Payload
sections.content:
The General Extension payload is defined in Section 6.15 of RFC 3830. This RFC adds Type 3, Key ID Information, which is not restricted to MBMS. The payload has the Next Payload, Type and Length fields of RFC 3830, followed by a variable-length Key ID Information field.

That field is made of Key ID Type sub-payloads. Each has a Key ID Type (8 bits), a Key ID Length in octets (8 bits) and the Key ID itself (variable length). There may be more than one sub-payload in an extension, and their total length cannot exceed 2^16 - 1 octets.

Three Key ID types are predefined for MBMS: value 0 for the Key Domain ID, 1 for the Service Key ID and 2 for the Traffic Key ID. Applications that use this payload may define new Key ID types and MUST define their semantics and usage according to the IANA section.
sections.plainLanguage: The label has a kind (domain, club or daily key), a length, and then the actual name. You can stick several labels on one message.

sections.title: The Empty Map Type
sections.content:
Sometimes security policy travels outside MIKEY. In the MBMS download case, each DRM Content Format object carries the parameters the receiver needs. MIKEY then has nothing to say about policy, so the RFC defines a CS ID map type value of 1, Empty map.

When the CS ID map type is set to this value, there MUST NOT be any Security Policy payload in the message.
sections.plainLanguage: If the instructions come in a different envelope, this message says so, and it carries no instruction page of its own.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Using MIKEY to update the traffic key by broadcast deviates from its original design. First, the MTK delivery is not source origin authenticated. It is protected by a group MAC keyed with the group key (MSK), so a group member could send fake MTK messages to other members. 3GPP judged the cost and difficulty of such an attack large enough compared to the expected gain that the risk was acceptable. Because of this, the extension is not compatible with SRTP-TESLA, which needs source origin authentication of the integrity key.

Second, MTK delivery is separate from security policy delivery. The policy arrives with the MSK. MTKs may be sent as often as a few seconds apart, so sending the policy with each would be costly in bandwidth. The policy is not expected to change during a session, but it can be updated by updating the MSK.

The Empty map type relies on the security provided by DCF, and MIKEY is only used to provide the master key for DCF processing.
sections.plainLanguage: Anyone in the club who knows the club key could fake a daily-key message. The designers decided that was too much trouble to be worth worrying about.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA registered value 3 for Key ID in the MIKEY General Extension Payload Type namespace. It also registered value 1 for Empty map in the CS ID map type namespace of the Common Header Payload.

A new namespace for the Key ID Type field was established, with the predefined types of Table 2. Values 0-240 SHOULD be approved by IETF consensus, and 241-255 are reserved for Private Use.
sections.plainLanguage: The new label kinds were written into an official list. Most future additions need group approval, and a few numbers are left free for private use.
